title: Tinea Pedis (Athlete's Foot)
subject: Microbiology & immunology
summary: A superficial fungal infection of the feet caused mainly by Trichophyton rubrum. It presents with itching, scaling and fissuring, especially between toes. Management relies on topical antifungals and hygiene.

sections.p: Tinea pedis is a dermatophyte infection of the skin and nails of the feet. It is common in hot, humid, low‑resource settings where footwear is tight and moisture accumulates.
b: Caused by Trichophyton rubrum (most common) and T. mentagrophytes
Often secondary to onychomycosis or tinea corporis
Predominant in adolescents and adults with poor foot hygiene

sections.p: Trichophyton species are keratinophilic moulds that grow at 25–30 °C. They produce hyphae that invade superficial keratinised layers.
b: Growth best on Sabouraud agar with chloramphenicol

sections.p: The fungus is transmitted by direct skin contact or via fomites such as shoes, socks, and communal showers. It survives in damp environments for months.
Tinea pedis manifests as erythema, scaling, fissuring, and sometimes blistering between toes and on the soles. Chronic infection can spread to nails.
Clinical diagnosis is usually sufficient. Confirmation can be obtained by potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation or fungal culture if atypical features are present.
b: Culture on Sabouraud agar confirms species

t.b: Detects fungal hyphae in scrapings; positive indicates dermatophyte infection
Identifies species; useful if lesions are atypical or treatment fails

sections.p: First‑line therapy is topical azoles (clotrimazole, terbinafine) applied twice daily for 2–4 weeks. In extensive disease, oral terbinafine may be required.
b: Topical azoles reduce fungal load and itching
Oral terbinafine preferred for severe or nail involvement
Maintain foot hygiene: dry feet, change socks daily

t.b: Treat superficial infection; avoid in patients with liver disease
Effective for extensive disease; monitor liver function if prolonged use

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, rely on history and inspection. Look for interdigital maceration, fissures, and nail changes. Avoid systemic therapy unless disease is widespread or nails involved.
b: Ask about footwear, sweating, and communal showers
Use KOH if available; otherwise treat empirically

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain, spreading lesions, signs of cellulitis (erythema, warmth, swelling), or systemic symptoms such as fever

faq.q: Can tinea pedis spread to other parts of the body?
faq.a: Yes, especially to the groin (tinea cruris) or hands if the patient touches the infected area.
It is contagious via direct contact or fomites; sharing towels or shoes increases risk.

faq.q: What if the patient has HIV?
faq.a: Immunosuppression may lead to more extensive disease and secondary bacterial infection; monitor closely.

exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with itchy, scaling skin between his toes. What is the most appropriate first‑line treatment? — Topical azole (clotrimazole or terbinafine) twice daily for 2–4 weeks; explain why systemic therapy is not first choice.

A patient with tinea pedis develops painful fissures and purulent discharge. What complication should you suspect and how would you manage it? — Secondary bacterial cellulitis; start empirical antibiotics (e.g., amoxicillin‑clavulanate) and treat the fungal infection.

A 35‑year‑old woman with chronic interdigital dermatitis refuses to change her footwear. What key advice would you give to prevent recurrence? — Wear breathable, loose shoes; keep feet dry; change socks daily; use antifungal powder.
A patient with tinea pedis reports no improvement after 4 weeks of topical therapy. What is the next step? — Consider oral terbinafine for 6 weeks; ensure compliance and monitor liver function.
A child presents with macerated skin between toes and a cracked nail. What additional diagnosis should be considered? — Onychomycosis; treat with oral terbinafine if nails are involved.

A patient with tinea pedis develops a red, swollen foot with fever. What urgent investigation is indicated? — Evaluate for cellulitis; obtain a swab for culture if purulent discharge is present and start antibiotics promptly.
